In the middle of the village there was a big stone cistern. It filled up with the winter rain, and the people of the village drank from it until the rain came back.

Uncle Abu Khalil looked after it. Every morning he filled two jars for each house — never giving one house more than another.

Lina came for her family's two jars with her little brother Karam. When she got home, she would pour some of the water over the courtyard to cool it, splash Karam so he laughed, and wash her doll's clothes twice every day.

Her mother told her, "Lina, this is the whole village's water, and there's a long summer between us and the rain."

Lina said, "The cistern is big, Mama. What difference does one jar make?"

Lina was not the only one who said that. In every house there was someone saying the same thing, and pouring out water just like she did.

Every evening Uncle Abu Khalil looked into the cistern, then walked away without saying anything.

Their neighbour, Auntie Umm Jamil, was an old woman who lived alone. When she made wudu, she collected the water in a bowl, and then watered the basil plant on her windowsill with it.

Lina watched her over the wall and wondered, saying to herself, "How careful she is with water!"

When summer grew hot, Uncle Abu Khalil let the bucket down into the cistern, and it did not reach the water until he had let out the whole rope.

He gathered the villagers and said, "From today, one jar for each house. If what's left is enough for us, we'll make it to the rain. If not, all we'll have is the faraway spring down in the valley."

Now one jar had to do for drinking, for kneading dough, and for wudu — everything. The heat grew stronger, and Karam got thirsty before the afternoon, and there was nothing left in the jar.

Lina went out to the courtyard and saw the ground where she had poured water for days, now dry and cracked. Not a trace of that water was left.

She sat by the door and cried. Auntie Umm Jamil saw her over the wall, called her over, and gave her a cup of water, saying, "This is what I have left from yesterday's jar."

Lina said, "But what about you, Auntie?" She said, "I know what summer is like, my dear. I only pour water where it does some good."

Lina gave her brother a drink, then went back to Auntie Umm Jamil and said, "Teach me."

From that day on, she covered the jar, drank from the small cup, and saved the leftover washing water to water the grapevine.

And whenever Karam splashed her, she said, "No, Karam — this is the village's water."

The summer days passed slowly and heavily. Every morning Uncle Abu Khalil filled the jars one by one, until there was only a little left at the bottom of the cistern.

Then one autumn morning the sky turned dark, and people heard thunder.

The villagers came out into the square. The rain poured into the cistern, and the children ran about under it.

Lina ran home, brought a big bowl, and put it where the rainwater came pouring off the roof. And Auntie Umm Jamil brought her bowl and put it right beside it.

﴿وَكُلُوا وَاشْرَبُوا وَلَا تُسْرِفُوا ۚ إِنَّهُ لَا يُحِبُّ الْمُسْرِفِينَ﴾

📖 Al-A'raf 31. This is a tale told as a parable; it did not happen to anyone in particular.
